newsitem.title: NEPAL: Nepalis vote in key parliamentary by-elections.
newsitem.headline: Nepalis vote in key parliamentary by-elections.

text.p: Nepalis were voting on Friday in parliamentary by-elections which analysts said could have serious implications for the survival of Prime Minister Sher Bahadur Deuba's coalition government.
Polling began at 8 a.m. (0215 GMT) in five constituencies scattered across four of the country's five regions.
The by-elections are the first popular vote since Deuba's centrist Nepali Congress party formed a fractious coalition government in September 1995.

Deuba narrowly survived a no-confidence motion last December after the opposition Unified Marxist-Leninist (UML) party split his coalition and mobilised 101 votes, two short of those needed to vote Deuba out in the 205-member parliament.

Deuba, who was weakened by a split in the Rastriya Prajatantra Party (RPP), a member of this three-party coalition, has vowed to seek a fresh vote of confidence, and has wooed back four RPP dissidents who broke away from his government.
Analysts see the outcome of Friday's ballots as crucial for Deuba ahead of his next test of strength with the communists.
The by-elections could change the balance of the Nepali Congress and the UML in parliament.

The UML, which has 87 deputies, is the largest party, but the Nepali Congress, which has 86 votes, commands a majority with the help of its partners: the RPP, which has 19 members, and the Nepal Sadbhavana Party (NSP), which has two deputies.
But the RPP is sharply divided over whether to continue supporting Deuba or joining the communists.
"It (the by-elections) is a fight over which party firmly establishes itself as the largest," said constitutional lawyer Badri Bahadur Karki.
Under Nepal's constitution, if Deuba lost the confidence vote and if the communists failed to provide an alternative, the single largest party could form a minority government.
The minority government would get 30 days to demonstrate its majority, failing which fresh polls would have to be held.
Parliamentary elections are not scheduled until 1999 in the kingdom, which ushered in multi-party rule in 1990 under a constitutional monarchy after a bloody pro-democracy movement.
